problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary  

**a. Verdict**  
I have obtained a complete solution.  
The minimum possible number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Permutation of uncovered squares** –  
   Because every row and every column must contain exactly one uncovered unit square, the set of uncovered squares is a *permutation matrix*: there is a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (\(n=2025\)) such that the uncovered squares are \((i,\pi(i))\).

2. **Left‑hand and right‑hand regions** –  
   For each row \(i\) define  
   \[
   L_i=\pi(i)-1,\qquad R_i=n-\pi(i),
   \]
   the numbers of covered cells to the left and to the right of the hole in that row.  
   The cells left of the holes form a Ferrers (Young) diagram whose row‑lengths are \((L_1,\dots ,L_n)\); the cells right of the holes form a Ferrers diagram with row‑lengths \((R_1,\dots ,R_n)\).

3. **Lower bound on the number of rectangles** –  
   The multiset \(\{L_i\}\) equals \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\) because the values \(\pi(i)\) run through \(1,\dots ,n\).  
   A classical fact (proved by a greedy algorithm) states that a Ferrers diagram can be partitioned into rectangles using exactly as many rectangles as there are *distinct positive* row‑lengths.  
   Since the distinct positive lengths among the \(L_i\) are \(1,2,\dots ,n-1\) (there are \(n-1\) of them), at least \(n-1\) rectangles are required to cover the left‑hand region.  
   The same argument applied to the right‑hand region (the multiset \(\{R_i\}\) is also \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\)) shows that at least another \(n-1\) rectangles are needed there.  
   Consequently any admissible tiling must contain at least  

   \[
   (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
   \]

   tiles.

4. **Construction attaining the bound** –  
   Choose the identity permutation \(\pi(i)=i\); the uncovered squares are the diagonal cells \((i,i)\).  

   *Left side*: for each row \(i=2,\dots ,n\) place a **single‑row rectangle** covering the cells \((i,1),(i,2),\dots ,(i,i-1)\).  
   This rectangle has height 1 and width \(i-1\); it lies entirely to the left of the diagonal hole in its row.  

   *Right side*: for each row \(i=1,\dots ,n-1\) place a **single‑row rectangle** covering the cells \((i,i+1),(i,i+2),\dots ,(i,n)\).  
   This rectangle also has height 1 and width \(n-i\); it lies entirely to the right of the diagonal hole in its row.  

   The two families consist of \((n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\) rectangles, they are pairwise disjoint (each occupies a distinct row), and together they cover every unit square except the diagonal ones.  
   Hence the construction satisfies the required condition with exactly \(2n-2\) tiles.

5. **Conclusion** –  
   The lower bound \(2n-2\) and the explicit construction both give the same number, so the minimum possible number of tiles is \(2n-2\).  
   For the given grid \(n=2025\),

   \[
   \boxed{2\cdot2025-2 = 4048}.
   \]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### Detailed Solution  

Let \(n=2025\).  
A placement of rectangular tiles (edges on grid lines, no overlaps) is required to leave exactly one uncovered unit square in each row and each column.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  Structure of the uncovered squares  

Because each row contains precisely one uncovered square and each column also contains precisely one, the set of uncovered squares is a *permutation matrix*: there exists a permutation \(\pi\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) such that  

\[
U=\{(i,\pi(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}
\]

is the set of uncovered unit squares.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  Left‑hand and right‑hand regions  

For a fixed permutation \(\pi\) define, for each row \(i\),

\[
L_i=\pi(i)-1\qquad\text{(cells left of the hole in row }i\text{)},
\]
\[
R_i=n-\pi(i)\qquad\text{(cells right of the hole in row }i\text{)}.
\]

The collection of cells left of the holes is the set  

\[
L=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le j\le L_i\}.
\]

If we view each row \(i\) as having length \(L_i\), the set \(L\) is exactly a Ferrers (Young) diagram whose row‑lengths are \((L_1,\dots ,L_n)\).  
Similarly, the cells right of the holes form a Ferrers diagram with row‑lengths \((R_1,\dots ,R_n)\).

Because \(\pi\) is a permutation, the numbers \(\pi(i)\) run through \(1,2,\dots ,n\); hence  

\[
\{L_i\}=\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\},\qquad \{R_i\}=\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  Lower bound on the number of rectangles  

**Lemma (Ferrers‑diagram rectangle partition).**  
Let a Ferrers diagram have row‑lengths \(a_1,\dots ,a_n\).  
The minimum number of axis‑parallel rectangles whose interiors are pairwise disjoint and whose union equals the diagram is exactly the number of *distinct positive* values among \(\{a_i\}\).

*Proof.*  
Order the rows so that the lengths are non‑increasing: \(b_1\ge b_2\ge\cdots\ge b_n\).  
Let \(c_1>c_2>\dots >c_k\) be the distinct positive lengths that occur.  
For each \(c_t\) take the rectangle consisting of all rows whose length is at least \(c_t\) and of the first \(c_t\) columns.  
These \(k\) rectangles are disjoint and together cover the whole diagram.  
Conversely, any rectangle can contain at most one of the distinct lengths as its rightmost column, because if a rectangle extended to column \(c_t\) it cannot also extend to column \(c_{t'}\) with \(c_{t'}>c_t\) (the latter columns are absent in some rows).  
Hence at least \(k\) rectangles are necessary. ∎

Applying the lemma to the left‑hand diagram, the distinct positive row‑lengths are \(1,2,\dots ,n-1\); there are \(n-1\) of them.  
Therefore at least \(n-1\) rectangles are required to cover all cells left of the holes.

The same reasoning applied to the right‑hand diagram (whose row‑lengths are also \(0,1,\dots ,n-1\)) shows that at least another \(n-1\) rectangles are needed there.

Consequently any admissible tiling must contain at least  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
\]

tiles.  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.  Construction with exactly \(2n-2\) tiles  

Choose the identity permutation \(\pi(i)=i\) for all \(i\).  
Thus the uncovered squares are the diagonal cells \((i,i)\).

*Left side.*  
For each row \(i=2,3,\dots ,n\) place a rectangle  

\[
T_i^{\text{L}}=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le j\le i-1\}.
\]

\(T_i^{\text{L}}\) has height 1 and width \(i-1\); it lies completely to the left of the diagonal hole in its row.  
The rectangles \(T_i^{\text{L}}\) are pairwise disjoint because they occupy different rows.  
Their union is precisely the set of all cells left of the diagonal.

*Right side.*  
For each row \(i=1,2,\dots ,n-1\) place a rectangle  

\[
T_i^{\text{R}}=\{(i,j)\mid i+1\le j\le n\}.
\]

\(T_i^{\text{R}}\) also has height 1 and width \(n-i\); it lies completely to the right of the diagonal hole in its row.  
These rectangles are again pairwise disjoint (different rows) and together cover all cells right of the diagonal.

Altogether we have  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
\]

rectangular tiles, they do not overlap, and every row and column contains exactly one uncovered square (the diagonal one).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.  Minimality  

The lower bound proved in §3 shows that no tiling can use fewer than \(2n-2\) tiles.  
The construction of §4 achieves this bound.  
Hence the bound is tight, and the minimum possible number of tiles equals \(2n-2\).

For the given grid \(n=2025\),

\[
\boxed{2\cdot2025-2 = 4048}.
\]
